title: Foreign Function Interfaces & Native Interop
summary: How managed runtimes call into, and are called from, native code — JNI's ceremony, P/Invoke's simplicity, and the real marshaling and memory-safety costs of crossing the boundary between a GC'd world and a raw-pointer one.

slides.markdown:
Every runtime in this group eventually needs to call code it didn't compile: a native image-processing library, an OS-level API with no managed wrapper, a performance-critical routine already written in C. A **foreign function interface (FFI)** is the mechanism that lets managed code call native code, and be called from it, safely (or at least survivably).

The two concrete FFIs this topic compares are Java's **JNI** and .NET's **P/Invoke** — same job, very different ergonomics. Both have to solve the same underlying problem: your runtime's objects and the native side's raw memory speak different languages, and someone has to translate at the boundary.

Three concrete reasons a managed program reaches for native code instead of staying entirely in its own runtime:

- **Reusing existing native libraries.** Decades of C/C++ libraries (codecs, crypto, image processing, drivers) exist and rewriting them in Java or C# isn't realistic.
- **Performance-critical code.** Some workloads (tight numeric kernels, SIMD-friendly loops) benefit from hand-tuned native code or from skipping GC and JIT overhead entirely.
- **OS-level access.** Some system calls and hardware interfaces have no managed equivalent and can only be reached by calling into native code that wraps the actual syscall.

None of these are exotic — most production Java or .NET codebases have at least one FFI boundary somewhere, even if most engineers on the team never touch it directly.

**JNI (Java Native Interface)** lets Java call native functions and vice versa, but demands real ceremony on both sides. On the Java side you declare a method `native` with no body; on the C side you implement a function with a specific, mangled name matching the Java class and method (`Java_com_example_Foo_bar`), and hand-write conversions between Java types and their native representations using JNI's C API (`JNIEnv*`, `jstring`, `jobject`, and so on).

A "hello world" JNI call — passing a Java `String`, doing something with it in C, returning an `int` — typically takes tens of lines of boilerplate on the native side alone. That verbosity is a real, well-known cost, and it's the main reason libraries like JNA and Project Panama's Foreign Function & Memory API exist to reduce it.

**P/Invoke (Platform Invoke)** takes a much lighter-weight approach: you declare an `extern` method with a `[DllImport]` attribute naming the native library and function, and the CLR generates the marshaling code for you at the call site — no hand-written native-side glue code required for straightforward cases.

```csharp
[DllImport("user32.dll")]
static extern int MessageBox(IntPtr hWnd, string text, string caption, uint type);
```

That's the entire binding for calling a native Win32 function — the CLR handles converting the C# `string` to the native representation the function expects. This is meaningfully less ceremony than JNI's approach, at the cost of less explicit control over exactly how marshaling happens for tricky types.

slides.markdown:
**Marshaling** is the conversion work happening at the boundary, and it's not free even when it's automatic. A managed `String` (UTF-16, garbage-collected, with a length prefix) isn't the same bytes as a native C string (a null-terminated byte array, manually managed) — every call across the boundary that passes a string does a real conversion, allocating a native buffer and copying data.

The same is true for arrays, structs with specific field layouts the native side expects, and object references, which can't cross the boundary directly at all — they get converted to handles or copied data instead. A tight loop calling a native function once per iteration pays this marshaling cost on *every* call, which is why FFI boundaries are usually designed for coarse-grained calls (one call doing a batch of work) rather than fine-grained ones (one call per element).

slides.sectionTitle: The GC can't see across the boundary
slides.subTitle: The leak that costs teams weeks
slides.markdown:
The most consequential FFI pitfall: native code allocates memory (via `malloc` or a native library's own allocator) on behalf of a managed object, and nothing on the managed side ever frees it, because the garbage collector only tracks managed heap memory — it has no visibility into memory a native call allocated.

This shows up as a slow, insidious leak: heap usage from the managed profiler's perspective looks perfectly healthy, while the process's actual OS-reported memory keeps climbing, because the leaking memory isn't in the GC's world at all. The fix requires explicit, disciplined cleanup — a `finalize`/`Dispose`-style pattern that calls a matching native `free` function, or (safer) wrapping the native handle in a `try/finally` or `using` block that guarantees release even on an exception. Forgetting this is genuinely common, because the managed-language habit of "the GC handles cleanup" doesn't extend past the FFI boundary.

slides.sectionTitle: JNI vs P/Invoke vs Rust's near-zero-cost FFI
slides.markdown:
| | JNI (Java) | P/Invoke (.NET) | Rust FFI (`extern "C"`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boilerplate | High — hand-written native glue code | Low — attribute-driven, CLR generates marshaling | Very low — types map close to C's directly |
| Type safety at the boundary | Weak — `jobject`/`jstring` are opaque handles | Moderate — the marshaler infers conversions | Strong, if the `unsafe` block is written correctly |
| Runtime overhead per call | Higher — JNI call overhead is a known JVM cost center | Lower, but non-zero (marshaling) | Near-zero — Rust has no separate managed heap or GC to bridge |

Rust's advantage here isn't magic — it's the direct consequence of `ahead-of-time-compilation-and-native-images`'s point about Rust having essentially no runtime to bridge from: there's no GC-to-native gap to marshal across, so `extern "C"` calls are close to a native call in cost.

JNI's verbosity was bad enough that the JDK shipped a direct replacement: the **Foreign Function & Memory API** (Project Panama, standardized in recent JDK releases) lets Java call native functions and manage native memory without hand-written C glue code or JNI's mangled-name convention — closer in spirit to P/Invoke's declarative style than to classic JNI.

The underlying problem this whole topic covers — a GC'd, managed world needing to safely cross into a raw-pointer, manually-managed one — doesn't go away with a nicer API. Panama still requires you to reason about native memory lifetimes explicitly (via `Arena`, its resource-scoping abstraction) precisely because the GC still can't see across the boundary; it just removes the boilerplate tax, not the fundamental safety responsibility.

"Call a native image-processing library from your Java service — plan and risk?" is a real interview prompt, and a complete answer covers:

1. **Which FFI mechanism** — classic JNI for maximum control, or the Foreign Function & Memory API for less boilerplate on a modern JDK.
2. **Call granularity** — batch the image data into one call rather than one call per pixel, since marshaling cost is paid per call.
3. **Memory ownership** — decide explicitly who allocates and who frees any native buffers, and wrap that lifecycle in a `try/finally`/`Arena`-scoped pattern so a leak isn't silent.
4. **Failure isolation** — a native crash (a segfault in the library) can take down the entire JVM process, unlike a Java exception; sandboxing or a separate process boundary is worth considering for an untrusted or unstable native library.

Naming all four, especially the memory-ownership and crash-isolation points, is what separates a working answer from a senior one.
